title: Why principles beat practices every time
author: Mark Enser
summary: Enser argues that CPD which specifies practices without teaching the principles behind them produces what he calls 'cargo cult teaching' -- the visible form of a strategy performed without the understanding that made it work, borrowing the term from Pacific islanders who built wooden runways after WWII hoping the supply planes would return. He uses Berliner's five-stage model of teaching expertise (built on the Dreyfus brothers' skill-acquisition framework) to argue that practice-only CPD keeps experienced teachers permanently at the novice stage, where behavior is rule-conforming and context-free, rather than developing the contextualized, flexible judgment that defines expert teachers. His central analogy is a route versus a map: a specified practice is a route that gets you to one destination and breaks the moment the road changes, while a principle is a map that lets a teacher navigate any classroom situation, recognize when a technique has become a crutch, and adapt on the fly. He draws on Shulman's pedagogical content knowledge and Priestley, Biesta and Robinson's account of teacher agency to argue that reducing teaching to specified practices treats it as a technical trade rather than a profession, and that this has a generational cost: if every cohort of teachers only ever inherits practices and not the principles beneath them, the profession's collective capacity to interrogate and improve its own methods erodes over time. The piece closes not as an argument against practices altogether, but for sequencing -- practices should be taught as illustrations of principles in action, alongside the evidence for why they work and the conditions under which they stop working.
points: Enser's core diagnostic is 'cargo cult teaching': CPD that mandates a visible practice (cold calling, exit tickets, sticky notes) without teaching the underlying principle produces compliance rather than adaptable craft, because teachers apply the ritual even where it doesn't fit the context.

He uses Berliner's expertise-development research to argue specified-practice CPD structurally traps experienced teachers at the novice stage -- rigid, rule-conforming behavior -- rather than accelerating them toward the contextualized, flexible judgment that defines expert teachers.

His route-versus-map analogy reframes the CPD design question: a route (practice) gets a teacher to one outcome and fails when conditions change; a map (principle) lets a teacher navigate to any outcome, including situations the original training never anticipated.

He frames the stakes as generational and professional, not just individual: a profession trained only in practices without principles is 'hollowing out its future,' because nobody remains who understands the reasoning well enough to revise or replace the next playbook.
quotes: This is cargo cult teaching. The term comes from the behaviour of Pacific island communities who, having watched supply planes land during the Second World War, built wooden runways and wore headphones made of coconut shells once the planes had gone. The ritual was perfect. The understanding of what made it work was absent.
The practice, separated from its principle, cannot adapt. And teaching is nothing if not a constant demand for adaptation.

The implication is stark. A CPD model built around practices is, by Berliner’s own framework, keeping teachers at the novice end of the developmental spectrum indefinitely. It does not accelerate expertise. It structurally prevents it.

A teacher who understands that worked examples should make expert thinking visible, not just display a finished product, can apply that principle across subjects, year groups and learning contexts... A teacher who has only been told to use worked examples has a route, and they will follow it whether or not it leads anywhere useful.
Every cohort of new teachers trained primarily in practices, without the principles beneath them, represents a narrowing of the profession’s intellectual base.
The question for school leaders is whether that is what they want. Whether they want teachers who can follow a playbook, or teachers who understand the game well enough to write one.
